text.brief: On January 27, 2023, Assistant Secretary of the Air Force Andrew Hunter wrote that a corn mill planned near Grand Forks Air Force Base posed a significant threat to national security.
text.record: Fufeng Group of Shandong had bought about 370 acres twelve miles from the base, which hosts drone and space communications units ([Witness statement (Daly), House Agriculture Committee hearing, 118th Congress (congress.gov)](https://www.congress.gov/118/meeting/house/116993/witnesses/HHRG-118-AG00-Wstate-DalyN-20240320.pdf)). CFIUS had concluded in December 2022 that it lacked jurisdiction over the purchase ([Senate committee hearing, 118th Congress (S. Hrg., CHRG-118shrg56337)](https://congress.gov/118/chrg/CHRG-118shrg56337/CHRG-118shrg56337.pdf)). The city council voted in February 2023 to stop the project. Treasury later brought land near the base under review, and a rule of November 2024 added 59 more installations to the list ([Federal Register, May 5, 2023: proposed rule adding military installations to 31 CFR Part 802 Appendix A (govinfo)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2023-05-05/pdf/2023-09259.pdf); [Federal Register, November 7, 2024: Definition of Military Installation and the List of Military Installations (Treasury final rule)](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/11/07/2024-25773/definition-of-military-installation-and-the-list-of-military-installations-in-the-regulations)).
text.reading: The review system measured ownership and missed geography, so a buyer from the mainland could place a permanent facility beside a strategic base with no federal check. A city council made a national security decision because no federal office owned it.
text.gapText: Architecture Governance. No federal office owned land deals near bases that sat outside the list, so the decision fell to local officials.
text.fix: Tie review of land purchases to the capabilities a base protects, and update the list as missions change.
